definition: Fallacious means based on unsound or misleading reasoning.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fallacious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fallacious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: His proof that the team wins whenever he wears the lucky socks is fallacious—the team also wins plenty of games while the socks stay home.
A shaky argument has weak spots a good editor might shore up; a fallacious one is built on a genuine logical flaw and cannot stand as reasoned.
Incoherent lies beyond fallacious: a fallacious argument at least hangs together well enough to fool someone, while an incoherent one offers no recognizable chain of reasoning at all.

Illogical means the steps of thinking go wrong — a conclusion that does not follow, a rule of sense broken along the way — and it can be entirely innocent. Fallacious adds a misleading edge: the flawed reasoning is dressed up to persuade, built well enough to take in a careless reader.

Unsound means resting on a defective foundation, whether the flaw sits in the facts or in the logic — a bridge design and an argument can both be unsound. Fallacious is the narrower verdict: the reasoning itself is broken, however true the individual facts may be.
built on solid evidence and correct steps
correctly reasoned, with conclusions that follow from the premises
No umpire is infallible; instant replay overturns a handful of calls every season.
Fallacious means based on unsound or misleading reasoning.

The debate coach circled the closing argument in red: 'Every great inventor was laughed at; people laugh at me; therefore I am a great inventor.' The reasoning is fallacious—being laughed at is shared by geniuses and crackpots alike, so it proves membership in neither group.
Fallacious is not the same as 'false': the speaker might even turn out to be a great inventor.
The word condemns the argument, not the conclusion—the logic is broken no matter how things end.
Fallacious is a precision tool for arguments and reasoning—essays, editorials, proofs.

Its neighbors in this unit split the work of 'false': spurious describes things and claims faked to look genuine, distortion names real facts twisted out of shape, and fallacious says the logic itself is broken.
A wrong phone number is merely incorrect, never fallacious.

At the regional science fair, the most confident poster belonged to a student who had played classical music to one tray of bean seedlings.
The music tray grew taller, the poster announced, therefore music makes beans grow.
A judge stopped and read it twice.
Her scorecard called the conclusion fallacious, and she was careful about the word: the measurements were accurate and neatly recorded.
The problem was the reasoning built on them.
The music tray also sat beside the window, so sunlight, not sound, could explain everything.
The argument looked persuasive, she wrote, and that was exactly the trouble -- it invited you to skip the step that failed.
